citations.text: Pillow, B. H. (2012). Children's discovery of the active mind: Phenomenological awareness, social experience, and knowledge about cognition. Springer.

en.general: What a person knows about mental activities such as attending, remembering, guessing and reasoning: that they exist, how they differ, how they work, and that people can read the same thing in different ways. In Pillow's account this knowledge builds from childhood through three kinds, knowing that an activity occurs, knowing how different activities relate to each other, and holding general assumptions about the nature of knowledge.

examples: A child says she is only guessing the answer and says that her friend, who watched, knows it.
A student explains that two readers saw different things in the same story because each took a different view.
nonExamples: Carrying out a memory strategy without any idea of how it works.
